name: SHM: period and restoring force
summary: For small swings, a pendulum's period T = 2π√(L/g) depends only on length and g, not amplitude or bob mass.

contrast_probes.probe: If you pull the same pendulum further out before letting go, does each swing take more time or less time?
contrast_probes.reply_if_first: More time, because it has a longer path to cover.
contrast_probes.reply_if_second: Less time, because it moves faster.

contrast_probes.probe: Two pendulums of the same length are released from the same small angle, one with a light bob and one with a heavy bob; would they stay in step?
contrast_probes.reply_if_first: Yes, they start from the same angle so they cover the same distance and stay together.
contrast_probes.reply_if_second: No, the heavy one will swing at a different speed and drift apart.

contrast_probes.probe: What would you change to make a pendulum come back sooner: release it from higher up, or hang a heavier bob?
contrast_probes.reply_if_first: Release it from higher up so it goes faster.
contrast_probes.reply_if_second: Hang a heavier bob, since mass changes the swing time.

contrast_probes.probe: A pendulum takes 2 s per swing at 4°; roughly how long does it take at 8°, still a small angle?
contrast_probes.reply_if_first: More than 2 s, maybe about 4 s, because it goes twice as far.
contrast_probes.reply_if_second: Still 2 s, because the time doesn't depend on how wide it swings.

contrast_probes.probe: A bob released from 10° moves faster at the bottom than one released from 5°; does that mean it finishes its swing first?
contrast_probes.reply_if_first: Yes, faster means it gets back first.
contrast_probes.reply_if_second: No, it also has farther to go, so both take the same time.

contrast_probes.probe: If you replace a 100 g bob with a 400 g bob on the same string, what happens to the period?
contrast_probes.reply_if_first: It changes, the heavier bob swings at a different rate.
contrast_probes.reply_if_second: It stays the same, because mass cancels and only L and g matter.

correct_exemplars: same time, because amplitude isn't in the formula
bigger swing goes further but also faster, so it evens out
only length and g matter for a pendulum
mass cancels out, so heavy or light gives the same period
both come back together as long as the angle is small
T is 2π root L by g, nothing else

name: SHM: velocity, acceleration, energy
summary: In SHM, speed peaks at the mean, acceleration peaks at the extremes, and total energy stays constant.

contrast_probes.probe: At the extreme point, which quantity of the block becomes zero: its acceleration or its total energy?
contrast_probes.reply_if_first: Its acceleration, because the block has stopped there.
contrast_probes.reply_if_second: Its total energy, because it has no speed there.

contrast_probes.probe: At the extreme point the block is at rest for an instant. Is its acceleration there zero, or the largest in the whole cycle?
contrast_probes.reply_if_first: Zero, because it isn't moving.
contrast_probes.reply_if_second: The largest, because the spring is stretched the most there.

contrast_probes.probe: Compare the block's total energy at the extreme point with its total energy at the mean position. Which is bigger?
contrast_probes.reply_if_first: The mean position, because it moves fastest there.
contrast_probes.reply_if_second: Neither, they are equal; only the KE and PE split is different.

correct_exemplars: at the extreme v is zero but a is max, ω²A
it stops for an instant but the spring is pulling hardest there
acceleration is zero only at the mean, where speed is max
total energy stays ½kA², it just shifts between KE and PE
at the ends it's all potential energy, in the middle all kinetic
no damping, so the total energy doesn't change during the swing

name: Waves are chained SHM; wave speed
summary: Each particle does SHM in place; the wave pattern moves at a speed set by the medium, not the source.

contrast_probes.probe: If you shake a rope faster, where does a red dot painted on its middle end up after a minute?
contrast_probes.reply_if_first: It gets carried down to the far end along with the wave.
contrast_probes.reply_if_second: It stays near its spot and just jiggles faster.

contrast_probes.probe: What decides how soon a pulse on a rope reaches the far end?
contrast_probes.reply_if_first: How fast the rope itself gets dragged forward.
contrast_probes.reply_if_second: How big the pulse is; a bigger one gets there sooner.

contrast_probes.probe: On the same rope, one pulse is tall but slowly made and the other is small but quickly made. Which reaches the end first?
contrast_probes.reply_if_first: The small, quickly made one.
contrast_probes.reply_if_second: The tall one.

contrast_probes.probe: After a wave has fully passed a ribbon tied to the middle of a rope, where is the ribbon?
contrast_probes.reply_if_first: Further along the rope, closer to the far end.
contrast_probes.reply_if_second: Back at the same spot; it only went up and down.

contrast_probes.probe: Same rope, same tension: you double how many times per second you shake it. What happens to the wave speed?
contrast_probes.reply_if_first: It doubles too.
contrast_probes.reply_if_second: It stays the same; the waves just get shorter.

contrast_probes.probe: Same rope, same tension: you make the pulse twice as tall. Does it reach the far end sooner?
contrast_probes.reply_if_first: Yes, the bigger pulse gets there sooner.
contrast_probes.reply_if_second: No, it arrives at the same time, just taller.

correct_exemplars: the rope just goes up and down, only the shape moves along
same rope, same tension, so same speed
speed depends on the medium, not on how I shake it
shaking faster only makes the waves shorter, not faster
a bigger wave has more energy but the same speed
the air just vibrates in place, the sound pattern is what travels

name: Superposition, standing waves, beats
summary: Overlapping waves add displacements, then pass on unchanged; close frequencies beat at |f1 − f2|.

contrast_probes.probe: Two equal and opposite pulses meet in the middle of a rope. A second later, is there any pulse near the ends?
contrast_probes.reply_if_first: No, nothing is left, the rope just stays flat.
contrast_probes.reply_if_second: Yes, each pulse is back near the end it started from.

contrast_probes.probe: Forks of 300 Hz and 304 Hz sound together. What happens to the loudness, and how often?
contrast_probes.reply_if_first: It keeps fading away because the waves cancel and the sound energy gets used up.
contrast_probes.reply_if_second: It throbs about 604 times a second.

contrast_probes.probe: Forks of 300 Hz and 304 Hz sound together. What happens to the loudness, and how often?
contrast_probes.reply_if_first: It keeps fading away because the waves cancel and the sound energy gets used up.
contrast_probes.reply_if_second: It throbs about 302 times a second.

contrast_probes.probe: Forks of 300 Hz and 304 Hz face each other across a room. Where their sound waves meet in the middle, what happens?
contrast_probes.reply_if_first: The waves bounce off each other and head back toward their own forks.
contrast_probes.reply_if_second: You hear a throb about 604 times a second.

contrast_probes.probe: Forks of 300 Hz and 304 Hz face each other across a room. Where their sound waves meet in the middle, what happens?
contrast_probes.reply_if_first: The waves bounce off each other and head back toward their own forks.
contrast_probes.reply_if_second: You hear a throb about 302 times a second.

contrast_probes.probe: Forks of 300 Hz and 304 Hz sound together. Roughly how many throbs per second do you hear?
contrast_probes.reply_if_first: About 604.
contrast_probes.reply_if_second: About 302.

contrast_probes.probe: At the instant two opposite pulses make the rope look flat, is the middle of the rope moving or still?
contrast_probes.reply_if_first: Still, the pulses have cancelled so nothing is happening there.
contrast_probes.reply_if_second: Moving fast, the energy is in its motion and the pulses come back out.

contrast_probes.probe: Kabir sends a tall pulse and Meera a short one toward each other on a slinky. After they meet, which pulse reaches Meera's end?
contrast_probes.reply_if_first: The short one, it bounces back to her.
contrast_probes.reply_if_second: The tall one, it passes straight through.

contrast_probes.probe: Forks of 300 Hz and 304 Hz sound together. Roughly how many throbs per second do you hear?
contrast_probes.reply_if_first: About 604.
contrast_probes.reply_if_second: About 4.

contrast_probes.probe: Forks of 300 Hz and 304 Hz sound together. Which number gives the pitch you hear, and which gives how often it throbs?
contrast_probes.reply_if_first: Both are about 302.
contrast_probes.reply_if_second: Pitch about 302 Hz, throbbing 4 times a second.

correct_exemplars: the beats are the difference, so 4 per second
they add while overlapping and then just carry on
the rope's flat but still moving, so the energy's still there
the pulses pass through each other unchanged
the average is the pitch, the difference is the beat rate
they go in and out of step, f1 minus f2 times a second

name: Reflection and mirrors
summary: A plane mirror forms a virtual, erect, same-size image as far behind the mirror as you are in front.

contrast_probes.probe: If you step 1 m back from a mirror, what happens to your image?
contrast_probes.reply_if_first: It looks farther away and I can see more of my body in it.
contrast_probes.reply_if_second: Nothing, it stays right there on the glass.

contrast_probes.probe: A small wall mirror shows you from head to chest. You walk three steps back. Down to where can you see now?
contrast_probes.reply_if_first: Lower down, maybe to my waist.
contrast_probes.reply_if_second: Still only down to my chest.

contrast_probes.probe: You stand 1 m from a mirror. How far from you is your image?
contrast_probes.reply_if_first: 1 m, because it's on the glass.
contrast_probes.reply_if_second: 2 m, because it's 1 m behind the glass.

correct_exemplars: the image is as far behind the mirror as I am in front
my image is double the distance from me, not on the glass
stepping back doesn't help, the image steps back too
you only need a mirror half your height
how much you see depends on the mirror's size and height, not how far you stand
angle in equals angle out from the normal, so the ray from my feet hits halfway down

name: Refraction and total internal reflection
summary: Light bends toward the normal entering a denser medium, away entering a rarer one; TIR needs denser-to-rarer travel beyond the critical angle.

contrast_probes.probe: A ray from air hits a pond at 70° to the normal, more than water's critical angle. What happens to it at the surface?
contrast_probes.reply_if_first: You expect it to enter and bend toward the normal; good, but would you say the same for a ray leaving water into air?
contrast_probes.reply_if_second: You expect it to be totally reflected; check which side of the surface the light starts on, and where it is denser.

contrast_probes.probe: A ray inside glass meets the glass-air surface at 20°. In the air, is its angle from the normal bigger or smaller than 20°?
contrast_probes.reply_if_first: You said smaller; ask yourself whether air is denser or rarer than glass, and what that does to the bending.
contrast_probes.reply_if_second: You said bigger; now, what would happen if that 20° grew past about 42°?

contrast_probes.probe: Can light coming from the air ever be totally internally reflected at a glass surface if you make the angle big enough?
contrast_probes.reply_if_first: You said yes; try it in Lens Bench from the air side at 80° and see whether any beam goes into the glass.
contrast_probes.reply_if_second: You said no; so what two things must be true for light to get trapped inside the glass?

correct_exemplars: denser to rarer it bends away, rarer to denser it bends toward
TIR only works going from the denser side out to the rarer side
you need denser to rarer and the angle bigger than critical, both
coming out of water into air it goes away from the normal
air into glass can never be TIR, it always gets in
if it hits straight along the normal it doesn't bend at all

name: Lenses and image formation
summary: A convex lens forms a full real image where rays meet, screen or not.

contrast_probes.probe: Half the lens is covered and the screen is taken away. What is left at the spot where the image was?
contrast_probes.reply_if_first: Half an image is still there at that spot.
contrast_probes.reply_if_second: Nothing at all, because the screen is gone.

contrast_probes.probe: The image is sharp on the screen. You stick paper over the top half of the lens. What changes on the screen?
contrast_probes.reply_if_first: Part of the image disappears and only half is left.
contrast_probes.reply_if_second: The whole image stays but gets dimmer.

contrast_probes.probe: You remove the screen and put your eye some distance beyond where the image was, looking at the lens. Do you see the image?
contrast_probes.reply_if_first: No, without the screen there is nothing to see.
contrast_probes.reply_if_second: Yes, I see the inverted image hanging in the air.

correct_exemplars: the full image still forms, just dimmer, because every part of the lens gets light from every point
the rays still meet at the same spot even if there's no screen
covering half the lens cuts the light, not the picture
the screen just lets us see it, the image is there anyway
half the lens means less light, so a fainter but complete image
if you put your eye beyond the image you could see it in the air

name: Interference (Young's double slit)
summary: Waves from two slits add or cancel, giving fringes of width beta = lambda D / d; energy is only redistributed.

contrast_probes.probe: When the slits are moved closer, what is the main thing that changes on the screen?
contrast_probes.reply_if_first: The fringes get narrower and more crowded.
contrast_probes.reply_if_second: More light energy gets made, so the bright fringes get brighter.

contrast_probes.probe: Ravi's screen now shows fewer, more crowded-looking fringes; did he move the slits closer or cover one slit?
contrast_probes.reply_if_first: He moved the slits closer, so the fringes squeezed together.
contrast_probes.reply_if_second: He covered one slit, so half the fringes went away.

contrast_probes.probe: After one slit is covered, what do you expect at the spot where the brightest fringe used to be?
contrast_probes.reply_if_first: Hardly any light, because that light was being made by the two beams interfering.
contrast_probes.reply_if_second: Still a bright fringe, the pattern is just cut down to half.

contrast_probes.probe: If Ananya halves the gap between the slits, what happens to the fringe width?
contrast_probes.reply_if_first: It halves too.
contrast_probes.reply_if_second: It doubles, because beta = lambda D / d.

contrast_probes.probe: The bright fringes are four times as bright as one slit alone; where did that extra light come from?
contrast_probes.reply_if_first: Interference created it.
contrast_probes.reply_if_second: It was taken from the dark fringes, so the total stays the same.

contrast_probes.probe: If one slit is taped over, will you still see alternating bright and dark fringes?
contrast_probes.reply_if_first: Yes, just half of them.
contrast_probes.reply_if_second: No, the fringes vanish and only a broad band of light from the open slit remains.

correct_exemplars: Fringe width is lambda D by d, so closer slits give wider fringes.
Interference only shifts light from dark bands to bright bands, total stays same.
Cover one slit and the fringes vanish, you just get a broad patch from that slit.
Bright where path difference is a whole number of wavelengths, dark at a half extra.
Bright ones go up to 4I0 and dark ones to zero, so it averages to 2I0.
Halving d doubles the fringe width.

name: Diffraction and polarization
summary: A narrower slit gives a wider central maximum, and a tilted polaroid between crossed polaroids lets some light through.

contrast_probes.probe: Which of these can make light reach a spot that was dark before: narrowing a slit, or adding a polaroid between two crossed polaroids?
contrast_probes.reply_if_first: Only the polaroid one — a narrower slit just makes the bright band thinner.
contrast_probes.reply_if_second: Only the narrower slit — a polaroid can only block light.

contrast_probes.probe: You halve the slit width. Does the first dark band on the screen move closer to the centre or farther away?
contrast_probes.reply_if_first: Closer, because the whole pattern shrinks with the slit.
contrast_probes.reply_if_second: Farther, because sin θ = λ/a doubles when a is halved.

contrast_probes.probe: Two crossed polaroids give a dark screen. You slide a third one at 45° between them. Does the screen stay dark or get some light?
contrast_probes.reply_if_first: It stays dark, because another polaroid can only block more.
contrast_probes.reply_if_second: It gets some light, I0/8, because the middle sheet turns the polarisation.

correct_exemplars: narrower slit makes the light spread more, so the central band gets wider
width is 2λD by a, so smaller a means bigger width
the middle polaroid turns the polarisation, so some light gets through the last one
with the 45 degree one in between you get I0 by 8, not zero
first minimum is at sin theta equals lambda by a, so smaller a pushes it out
a polaroid passes the part along its axis, it doesn't just block
